The Delhi High Court has granted interim protection to actress and member of parliament Kangana Ranaut.

The order, dated October 8 and reported today, addresses unauthorized uses of her name, image, voice and other identifying attributes.

The case includes allegations involving AI-generated deepfakes, fabricated speeches, manipulated videos and false endorsements.

The court directed Meta to remove identified infringing material within 72 hours of receiving the order.

It also directed government departments to take steps concerning specified websites.

The ruling is interim. The underlying case hasn't been finally decided.

What interests me is the enforcement mechanism.

For someone targeted by AI impersonation, establishing that content is unauthorized is only part of the problem.

Then comes the practical work.

Find the content.

Identify where it's hosted.

Report it.

Explain the violation.

Wait for a response.

Discover another copy.

Repeat.

For a public figure, that process can become endless.

A manipulated video can be copied to dozens of accounts before the original disappears.

The Delhi court's order gives Ranaut a route to notify defendants about additional infringing material without filing an entirely new lawsuit each time.

That matters.

But it also exposes a limitation in how we currently protect people from digital impersonation.

Most enforcement begins after the unauthorized representation has already been published.

By then, people may have seen it.

Some may believe it.

Others may have downloaded it.

The person whose likeness was used is left trying to contain the damage.

I think we need to distinguish three separate responsibilities.

The creator should have a legitimate basis for using someone's likeness.

The platform should respond appropriately when unlawful impersonation is identified.

And the person being represented should have a practical way to establish which uses they've authorized.

That third part remains underdeveloped.

A creator can authorize a synthetic advertisement.

A politician can authorize an AI-generated campaign video.

An actor can license a digital representation for a film.

Those uses need clear records of permission.

The same records could help platforms distinguish authorized uses from unauthorized commercial impersonation.

Of course, legal protection has limits.

Satire, criticism, journalism and political expression raise legitimate free-speech concerns.

An identity protection system shouldn't become a tool for suppressing lawful criticism.

The challenge is creating rules that address deceptive impersonation without giving public figures control over every depiction of themselves.

The Delhi court's order is a concrete response to a specific dispute.

The larger problem is that people still have limited practical tools for proving which digital representations they actually authorized.

And AI has made creating those representations extraordinarily easy.

IEC enters into partnership to counter disinformation | @SAgovnews

October 20, 2026

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has entered into a partnership with Google, Meta, Microsoft, TikTok and non-profit organisation, Moxii Africa, to ensure the integrity of election information and counter disinformation ahead of the 4 November 2026 Local Government Elections.

The partnership is a sequel to a similar framework signed with the platforms ahead of the 2024 National and Provincial Elections (NPE). It is an indispensable lever buttressing the Commission’s purposive measures to enhance the integrity of election information.

These measures include the gazetting of the Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections (the Disinformation Code), on 4 September 2026.

The Code applies to political parties, candidates and anyone acting on their behalf. It forms part of the Electoral Code of Conduct and carries the same sanctions. 

According to the Commission, the partnership brings the platforms into the same effort to keep election information accurate and trustworthy.

Underscoring the importance of the partnership, the Commission’s Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo said the strategic inclusion of the online platforms gives the Commission direct access to the platforms and a real fighting chance against disinformation.

“Our partnership with digital platforms is critical to ensuring that voters have access to credible, accurate and trustworthy information to make informed political choices. A technically flawless election can still lose public trust if citizens are overwhelmed by disinformation.

“Therefore, the partnership eliminates barriers to direct access to the platforms and enables instantaneous remedial action against disinformation peddlers,” Mamabolo said.

The partnership covers the following:
• Cooperation in good faith during the election period;
• Respect for existing laws, with no requirement to share confidential user data;
• Alignment with the Constitution, municipal electoral laws and the Electoral Code of Conduct, including the Disinformation Code;
• A working group of partners, election awareness campaigns, and training on disinformation for political parties, candidates and other stakeholders;
• Room for platforms to apply their own policies, including content removal, advisory warnings and delisting, and
• Cooperation on other initiatives intended to curb the impact of disinformation in elections.
 The Commission has designated the Real411 platform to support its proactive efforts to minimise the impact of disinformation during the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Anyone who sees suspected election-related disinformation can report it to Real411 at https://t.co/Kc7kXVrgbE or through the Real411 app.

Complaints are handled in all eleven official languages. Real411 assesses complaints independently and recommends action to the Commission and the platforms.

Depending on the findings, the Commission, upon careful review of any reported complaint indicating disinformation or misinformation, can: 
• Refer the matter to the Electoral Court, which can impose sanctions. 
• Promptly refer the matter to the relevant online platform, which is expected to prioritise referrals from the Commission by acknowledging and swiftly processing the notification in line with its policies. 
• Issue media statements to alert the public and correct the disinformation. Guidance for voters on spotting, checking and reporting disinformation is available at https://t.co/7XX2mAKHXp.

The partners welcomed the partnership and reaffirmed their commitment to working with the Commission. They noted that they already have policies and mechanisms to counter disinformation and will keep using them as part of the collective effort.

“Free, fair and credible elections depend on people being able to trust the information they see. No single organisation can tackle disinformation alone, which is why Microsoft is pleased to join the Electoral Commission in this partnership.

“Ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, we will work alongside the Commission, civil society and industry to help voters find authoritative election information, strengthen media and AI literacy, and counter deceptive AI-generated content,” said Director: Government Affairs, Microsoft South Africa, Abongile Vanda in affirming Microsoft’s support for the partnership.

“At TikTok, we recognise the important role our platform plays in helping people discover information and engage in public conversations. This is why we take our responsibility to protect our community during elections very seriously.

“Through our in-app Election Centre, South Africans will be able to access reliable information about the elections, and to further support this, we have introduced election-related labels and search banners that direct users to the centre with a single tap.

“This work is supported by advanced moderation, collaboration with fact-checking partners and electoral commissions like the IEC South Africa to ensure a safe, informed, and authentic election experience for our community,” TikTok’s Government Relations and Public Policy Lead for Southern Africa, Tholoana Ncheke-Mahlaela, said.

“Information integrity is fundamental to the credibility of any democratic process. In an increasingly complex digital environment, protecting voters from misinformation and disinformation requires coordinated action across institutions, technology platforms, civil society and citizens themselves.

“This partnership represents an important commitment to ensuring that South Africans can access accurate, trustworthy election information and participate in the 2026 Local Government Elections with confidence,” Moxii Africa Director William Bird welcoming the partnership.

Bird said he is proud to support this collective effort to strengthen trust, transparency and democratic resilience.

The only other person who’s ever made me this excited about a product unveil was Steve Jobs. Watching him introduce the first iPhone is a huge part of why I fell in love with technology.

Elon brings that feeling back for me, but honestly, I think he takes it to a whole different level. Tomorrow, he and the Tesla team are unveiling the next-gen Roadster, and I seriously cannot wait. 

The Roadster they showed in 2017 already promised 0–60 mph in 1.9 seconds. Since then, Elon has talked about a Tesla–SpaceX collaboration, having it fly, and getting that time below ONE second, and calling it “the least interesting part” of the car. 

How do you say something like that and expect me NOT to be excited?!

But beyond how fast it goes, I want to see something that makes me sit there and say, “Wow… how in the world did they build that?” I honestly don’t know what they’re going to show us, and that’s part of what makes this so much fun. I really want to be surprised and see the unthinkable.

These days I feel many older people don’t get that excited about things… I only see that spark in kids. But imo, we should still get excited about people building cool things. We should still root for the nerds, engineers, and designers trying to do something that has never been done before.

And I hope there’s a kid watching tomorrow who feels what I felt watching Steve Jobs introduce the iPhone. Someone who sees this car and starts wondering how it works, sketching their own ideas, or thinking about what they could build someday.

I hope y’all are ready to have your minds blown. 

I’m rooting for you, Elon, and the entire Tesla team behind this car. 

Go give us a night we’ll never forget!

text:
Open Letter to Elon Musk: Who Controls the Signal?
Sovereignty, Selective Outrage, and the Real Costs of Private Connectivity

Dear @ElonMusk,

Things are rarely pure coincidence when timing, platforms, and pressure align against a state’s control of its own communications and industrial backbone. Toolkits, timed reports, selective outrage, and spontaneous amplification on the same platforms have long been used to loosen sovereign oversight of critical infrastructure. When a private operator holds the ability to enable, restrict, or reroute connectivity above national borders, the stakes move from market access to national security. Democracies worldwide face the same question. Who decides when the signal stays on, and under whose law?

Your recent posts on India illustrate the pattern. The sequence began with references to "unnamed oligarchs" maintaining a "monopolistic chokehold" on Indian people. It moved to a direct question asking whether Mukesh Ambani is the "real boss" of India. It continued with a sarcastic address to "Prime Minister Ambani" suggesting monopolistic exploitation. 

India’s Ministry of Communications has stated that its satellite communications framework is fair and non-discriminatory. Three licensees, including Starlink, remain at comparable stages pending security clearances from the Home Ministry and spectrum assignment. Starlink received its GMPCS licence and IN-SPACe approval earlier. Final security conditions, including lawful interception, data routing through Indian gateways, and local storage requirements, remain outstanding. These rules trace in part to the 2008 Mumbai attacks, in which satellite phones were used by the perpetrators. Regulatory caution is not new. Framing a security process as personal capture of the economy is.

Certain profiles receive selective amplification in these sequences. Engagement with disgruntled voices inside India, including responses that welcome the outsider and gesture toward further targets, fits a broader pattern of treating regulatory caution as evidence of capture. Some amplify the charge while remaining silent on identical restrictions applied by other states and on the documented dual-use record.

Your selective silence is notable. Mainland China has never licensed Starlink. Terminals are prohibited equipment. Traffic does not route through Chinese gateways. Beijing treats the constellation as a dual-use national security concern because of foreign control and potential military application. Your substantial Tesla operations in China have not produced equivalent public campaigns against that ban. The same contrast appears with Huawei, ZTE, and TikTok. The United States and multiple allies restricted or banned those systems on documented grounds of equipment risk, data access by foreign governments, and dual-use potential. National security arguments are applied rigorously against some foreign networks and treated as obstacles when applied to others.

Documented criminal adaptation supplies concrete evidence of the risk. In November 2024, Indian authorities intercepted a Myanmarese trawler near Barren Island carrying approximately 6,000 kilograms of methamphetamine. A Starlink Mini terminal was recovered. Investigators stated the smugglers used it for navigation and encrypted messaging with Golden Triangle handlers. In July 2025 the Colombian Navy seized an unmanned semi-submersible equipped with a Starlink antenna and linked to the Gulf Clan, assessed as a test for remote cocaine transport. Similar terminals have been documented at illegal gold mining sites in Brazil’s Amazon, leading authorities to require identification for new users in the region. In Myanmar, Starlink terminals powered scam compounds involved in human trafficking and cyber-fraud. SpaceX has stated it disabled more than 2,500 kits near suspected centers. Nigerian troops have reported intercepting hundreds of devices allegedly used by Boko Haram and ISWAP. These are reported seizures and operational adaptations spanning 2024 to 2026.

The Ukraine case remains the clearest demonstration of private control over a sovereign military operation. After the 2022 Viasat disruption, Starlink became essential for Ukrainian communications. In September 2022 Ukrainian forces sought coverage near Sevastopol for a maritime drone operation against the Russian Black Sea Fleet. You declined, stating that enabling it would make SpaceX explicitly complicit in a major act of war. Coverage over Crimea had not been active. The request was refused. Ukrainian drones lost their link. The episode showed that a single private decision determined the reach of a military action by a country at war. Russian forces have since used smuggled terminals to extend drone ranges. SpaceX has worked with Ukrainian authorities to geofence some misuse. The dependency and the discretion both exist.

A parallel form of external pressure has targeted large indigenous industrial groups. The Adani Group is one of India’s largest infrastructure conglomerates, with major positions in ports, airports, power, and logistics. In January 2023, Hindenburg Research published a report accusing the group of stock manipulation and opaque offshore structures, describing it as the largest con in corporate history. Adani denied the claims. Within days listed stocks lost more than $100 billion in market value at the lowest point. A major public offering was cancelled. Indian reporting later described the group’s response as "Operation Zeppelin", combining legal, cyber, and investigative efforts, with noted collaboration with Israeli-linked intermediaries. The report appeared days before Adani was set to close a $1.2 billion deal for a stake in Israel’s Haifa port. Hindenburg Research closed operations in January 2025. Adani stocks later recovered a substantial portion of the lost value. The short-term damage to valuations and project timelines was nonetheless measurable. Were it not for the deep ties and collaboration between India and Israel, this major risk might never have been thwarted.

The pattern of external reports timed against strategic industrial groups appears in other Global South markets. In 2023 Hindenburg published a report on Nigeria-focused Tingo Group, a Nasdaq-listed agri-fintech company, calling the business an exceptionally obvious scam. Tingo’s shares fell more than 50 percent in a single session. The company disputed the claims. Similar short reports have targeted other cross-listed emerging-market firms. In each case selling pressure and delayed capital raises hit companies whose primary operations sit outside deep Western capital markets. For infrastructure-heavy groups the result can be slower expansion of ports, energy capacity, or connectivity that governments treat as national priorities.

These patterns carry implications for democracies everywhere. Low-Earth-orbit systems bypass terrestrial gateways that states traditionally use for lawful interception, data residency, and emergency control. A private operator can apply geographic limits or refuse extensions based on its own judgment. External research reports can erase billions in market value in days. Gray markets move hardware faster than regulation. Countries that restricted Huawei or similar equipment did so because foreign control of critical communications creates leverage during crisis. The same logic applies when the operator is commercial. Bolivia moved from years of refusal on sovereignty grounds to rapid licensing after a change in government. Other nations have gone further, filing complaints with the ITU over unauthorized transmissions into their territory. Multiple states continue to require local gateways and security clearances before commercial service. These are responses to observed dual-use and criminal diversion.

Pressure campaigns that treat security clearances as corruption, amplify selective free-speech claims, and ignore identical restrictions elsewhere follow a recognizable sequence. Connectivity benefits are real in remote areas and disaster zones. So are the documented uses by cartels and non-state groups, the demonstrated ability of one company to decide coverage in an active conflict, and the measurable economic cost of sudden valuation shocks to indigenous industrial capacity. 

Democracies that value both open information and sovereign control of critical infrastructure face the same tension. Consistency in applying national security standards would strengthen rather than weaken the case for expanding access. The pattern is visible to those who compare the cases rather than the slogans. 

Eyes open. Dates and decisions still matter.

Respectfully,

Concerned observers of democracy, digital rights, and sovereignty

text:
Polymarket has been blocked in India due to legal action by the Indian government. The platform itself hasn't taken any direct action against Indian users.

What happened?

In 2025, India passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act (PROGA), which came into effect on May 1, 2026. The law prohibits real-money online games, including betting and prediction markets. Platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi fall under this category.

1\. On April 25, 2026, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology reportedly directed VPN providers and intermediaries to restrict access to platforms like Polymarket.

2\. By May 2026, ISPs had blocked Polymarket at the DNS level. Many Indian users could no longer access the website.

3\. Polymarket itself didn't list India as a restricted country and had previously allowed users to sign up. However, government restrictions affected access.

4\. In October 2026, Polymarket's official X account was also reportedly withheld in India following a legal demand, preventing many Indian users from viewing its posts.

In short: Polymarket hasn't reportedly taken users' money or frozen their accounts specifically because they are Indian. The restrictions came from the Indian government, which blocked access to the platform and reportedly restricted its X account as well.

INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

By Skye Jacobs  Today 2:36 PM    
Your ChatGPT conversations could end up in court, and they're not protected
Chatbot conversations lack the legal privilege covering communications with lawyers, doctors, and therapists

 Add TechSpot 
   📷
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.  
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust.
The takeaway: Private  conversations with AI chatbots are increasingly being used in court  cases, creating a new source of evidence for police, prosecutors, and  civil litigants. These records can expose a user's intentions, private  thoughts, and sensitive disclosures, yet they generally receive none of  the legal confidentiality protections afforded to conversations with  lawyers, doctors, or therapists.
ChatGPT and similar tools are often used for personal questions, legal worries, health concerns, and emotional support. Those conversations can feel private, but they may be accessible through a phone search, a  subpoena, discovery in a lawsuit, or a report by the AI company itself.

A review by The Washington Post found chatbot conversations cited in  12 public court cases over the past two years. The number is likely  higher because much of the evidence collected during investigations and  lawsuits never becomes public.

One case involved a teenager identified in court records as R.K.C.,  who sued Meta, Snap, TikTok, and YouTube in 2023. He alleged that their  platforms contributed to social media addiction and mental health  problems.

Defense lawyers obtained his ChatGPT history during the case. In one  October 2024 conversation, R.K.C. asked the chatbot to explain a  statement from his father about a possible settlement.

"My dad Said that I'm will get a settlement worth of  1million dollar," he wrote. "He said that If that doesn't make me happy  what does. What does he mean."

// Related Stories

 Ring rolls out new encryption system that could limit what it can hand over to police 
 AI is driving an "expertise recession" as people increasingly question professional advice 

R.K.C.'s lawyers settled with Snap, TikTok, and YouTube by late July.  They also dropped the case against Meta, saying they were concerned  about putting the teenager through a long trial. The companies denied  his claims. Mike Morgan, a partner at Morgan & Morgan, said the  ChatGPT messages did not affect the outcome of the case.
📷

Credit: The Washington Post

Morgan said young people may share more with a  chatbot than they would with family members, friends, or therapists. "A  fifteen-year-old may type things into a chatbot that he may not say to a  therapist, a parent, or a friend, and he does it without realizing that  it could end up in a defense expert's report," he said in a statement.

Chatbot records have also become part of criminal cases.

In Palm Beach County, Florida, OpenAI contacted the  FBI after a ChatGPT user repeatedly described plans to harm an  ex-girlfriend, according to a police affidavit. The FBI passed the  information to local police, who identified the woman and found that the  user, Darren Zhou, had sent her anonymous messages after their  relationship ended.

Police said the ChatGPT conversations supported the  credibility of the threats. Zhou was arrested in May and charged with  stalking and making electronic threats. He pleaded guilty this month and  was sentenced to eight years of probation.

OpenAI has said it uses software to detect  conversations that may involve dangerous behavior. Those conversations  can be reviewed by staff. If reviewers determine there is "an imminent  and credible risk of harm to others," the company may contact law  enforcement.

The company has not said how often it makes such  reports. Its transparency data, however, shows a sharp increase in  government and law-enforcement requests for user information. OpenAI  disclosed data from more than 80 accounts during the second half of  2025, more than four times the total from the same period a year  earlier.

In many cases, police do not need to obtain records from an AI company. They find the conversations on a person's phone.

Michael Price, litigation director of the Fourth  Amendment Center at the National Association of Criminal Defense  Lawyers, said people often agree to let officers search their phones. In  most situations, people have the right to refuse a search unless police  have a warrant.

"The short answer is that most people consent," Price told The Washington Post. "They shouldn't, but they do."

📷

That happened in the case of Ryan Schaefer, a  Missouri State University student accused of damaging 17 cars in a  campus parking lot. According to police records, Schaefer agreed to let  officers search his phone. They found ChatGPT messages he sent shortly  after the alleged vandalism.

"How f----d am i bro," Schaefer wrote. "What if i smahsed the s--- oitta mutlipls cars."

He later wrote: "Is there any way they could know it was me."

Schaefer later pleaded guilty to felony property damage and was sentenced in July to five years of probation.

AI chats can also be pulled into civil lawsuits  through the discovery process. In a Michigan employment case, a tire  salesman's former employer alleged that he had taken customers after  joining a rival company. The salesman had asked ChatGPT whether deleted  Yahoo emails could still be retrieved, including through a court  subpoena.

The employer argued that the messages showed he had  tried to hide evidence. A judge later ordered him to pay an undetermined  amount in attorneys' fees and allowed the lawsuit to continue.

Chatbot exchanges do not have the legal protections  that apply to conversations with lawyers, doctors, or therapists. OpenAI  CEO Sam Altman has said AI conversations should have stronger privacy  protections because people increasingly use chatbots for sensitive  matters. Courts have not recognized that type of privilege.

A federal judge in New York made that clear in a case  involving financial executive Bradley Heppner. Heppner argued that  prosecutors should not be allowed to review his conversations with  Anthropic's Claude about potential fraud defenses. The judge ruled that  the chats were not protected because Claude is not a lawyer and  Heppner's attorneys had not told him to consult the chatbot.

Heppner was convicted in May of securities fraud, wire fraud, and other charges.

The issue may grow as AI tools take on more tasks for  users and gain access to more personal data. Andrew Ferguson, a law  professor at George Washington University who studies digital  surveillance, said chatbot records may be only the beginning.

"Your entire world is going to now be available for police," Ferguson said.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

IFF statement against the Alarming Escalation of Social Media Censorship and Proposed Expansion of Takedown Powers

New Delhi, March 19, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by continuing reports of posts and accounts being withheld in India on Facebook, X and Instagram, including satire and criticism of the government. Recent reporting shows users receiving generic “withheld in India” notices or emails under Section 69A from social media platforms, with little or no explanation, while independent reporting has documented takedowns affecting speech that appears political, satirical, or critical rather than clearly unlawful.

As reported by Business Standard and The Indian Express on March 18, the Union Government is currently exploring a proposal to decentralize content blocking powers under Section 69A of the IT Act. The new proposal would grant direct takedown powers to multiple ministries, including Defence, Home Affairs, External Affairs, and Information & Broadcasting. At present, MeitY signs off on Section 69A orders, while a separate notice and takedown channel already operates through Section 79(3)(b) and the Home Ministry led Sahyog portal that at least has 35 nodal officers across State Police Departments in India.

At the same time, the February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules have sharply compressed compliance timelines. MeitY’s own published FAQ says intermediaries must act within 3 hours when they receive actual knowledge through a court order or a government intimation, within 36 hours for certain expedited grievances, and within 2 hours for specified complaints involving nudity, sexual content, morphed content, and impersonation. The government has also reiterated that intermediaries which fail to observe due diligence risk losing Section 79 immunity. A system built on speed, legal threat, and secrecy predictably incentivises over compliance.

We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A in the Shreya Singhal case on the basis of procedural safeguards and written reasons that could be challenged. Secret and inaccessible censorship defeats those safeguards in practice. 

IFF calls on the Union government to halt any move to decentralise Section 69A blocking powers further, publish blocking orders with only as per the letter and spirit of the Shreya Singhal judgement, and ensure timely notice to affected users with clear grounds and avenues for remedy. Platforms must also do more than send boilerplate messages. They should provide meaningful notice, preserve records for challenge, and publish granular transparency reporting given online censorship also impacts the public right to receive information.

If your account or post has been withheld or blocked in India, please write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots, URLs, and any email or platform notice you have received. IFF will try to assist impacted users and document patterns of opaque censorship.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
INDIA TO IDENTIFY ALL TELEGRAM, WHATSAPP AND SIGNAL USERS WITH "SIM BINDING"

India is set to enforce "SIM binding" for major messaging apps from around January 1, 2027.

What is the ruling

The Department of Telecommunications (@DoT_India) directed platforms including WhatsApp (@WhatsApp), Telegram (@telegram), Signal (@signalapp), Snapchat (@Snapchat), others in 2025 to keep accounts continuously linked to the specific active SIM used for registration.

If that SIM is removed, deactivated or swapped, the app should stop working on the device until the correct SIM is present and verified.

iOS has long blocked apps from directly reading SIM status or hardware identifiers. Apple (@Apple) released a software patch in September that lets apps detect when an iPhone lacks a SIM card, making compliance possible for messaging apps. Apple has not issued a detailed public statement on its reasoning. Earlier queries to the company went unanswered.

What it means for online privacy

The rule does not break end-to-end encryption. It does, however, strengthen the permanent link between a messaging account, a telecom-issued phone number, and the owner's identity.

The Department of Telecommunications runs platforms such as the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and Sanchar Saathi (TAFCOP). These aggregate connection data across operators so authorities can see how SIMs are linked to an individual's verified identity.

Claimed motivation

The government want to identify everyone online.

The government says the rule closes a loophole that lets accounts keep working after the SIM is removed or the number is used from abroad. This has been exploited for phishing, impersonation, "digital arrest" scams and other fraud. Officials cite large cyber-fraud losses and argue that tying accounts to KYC-verified telecom identities improves traceability, similar to existing SIM/device binding already used in banking and UPI (@NPCI_NPCI) apps.

Experts' opinion

Fraudsters routinely obtain SIMs with weak or fake KYC, use them briefly, and discard them. Binding does little against that or against malware, phishing kits and session hijacking.

Industry groups such as IAMAI (@IAMAIForum) have argued the rule mainly creates friction for ordinary users while leaving core attack vectors largely intact,

India's record on using online deanonymising tools

India has a documented pattern of using legal, technical, and policing tools to restrict online speech, target critics, and limit communications during protests—actions frequently criticized by human-rights organisations as disproportionate or politically selective. The new SIM-binding and related telecom identification rules increase the technical capacity to track identity-linked communications, raising the practical risk of similar misuse even if the stated purpose is "fraud prevention".

Reporters Without Borders (@RSF_inter) ranked India 157th out of 180 in its 2026 World Press Freedom Index. RSF and others cite violence against journalists, heavy concentration of media ownership linked to figures close to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (@BJP4India), and the increasing use of criminal laws against reporters and critics.

Section 69A of the IT Act is the main blocking tool. In 2026, orders have targeted satirical cartoons critical of the prime minister, fact-checker posts, media outlets such as The Wire (@thewire_in), and accounts posting political criticism or mockery.

In October 2026, during demonstrations in Delhi linked to voter-roll revisions and the "Cockroach Janta Party" movement, which criticised the Election Commission (@ECISVEEP), authorities imposed mobile-internet blackouts, conducted mass detentions (including opposition leaders such as Rahul Gandhi and journalists, and reportedly monitored messaging groups.

What can concerned Indians do?

Practical steps for Indians concerned about online privacy are limited by mandatory SIM ID checks, biometric rules, and SIM-binding requirements, but they can still meaningfully reduce exposure.

True anonymity is difficult in India because almost all consumer SIMs are tied to verified identity through ID checks and increasingly biometric checks.

👉 Prefer Signal for sensitive conversations. It has stronger default end-to-end encryption and collects less metadata than WhatsApp. Both will still be subject to SIM-binding, but Signal's design is more privacy-oriented.

👉 Use a reputable no-logs VPN (Mullvad (@mullvadnet), Proton VPN (@ProtonVPN) for sensitive browsing or public Wi-Fi. Note that CERT-In (@IndianCERT) logging rules led most privacy-focused providers to remove physical servers from India; many now offer virtual Indian IPs hosted abroad.

👉 Enable disappearing messages, turn off read receipts where possible, and verify safety numbers for important contacts.

👉 Restrict who can see your phone number, profile photo, last seen, and "about" status (set to "My contacts" or "Nobody").

👉 Avoid using the same number for banking, government services, and casual or sensitive chats if you can manage a second number within the legal 9-SIM limit.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s Statement on eMudhra Private Key Vulnerability

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is concerned about the wider cybersecurity consequences of the recently discovered security vulnerability relating to eight intermediate certificates issued by the Indian digital certification company, eMudhra. This development prompted @Google, @mozilla and @Cloudflare to block the compromisable certificates.

As per Google and Mozilla’s reports, it was found that the private keys linked to the eight affected eMudhra certificates were generated with insufficient randomness. The keys contained severely truncated or trivial key values, with key strength measuring as small as four to eight bits rather than standard cryptographic requirements like RSA-2048 or ECC P-256. This could provide bad actors with ammunition to recover private keys, use them to create fraudulent certificates, impersonate legitimate websites and potentially intercept or modify communications.

The incident raises serious questions about the technical safeguards employed to protect India's public key infrastructure. Digital certificates are a foundational component of internet security, as they enable users to verify the identity of websites and establish encrypted connections with online services. This includes services that utilise sensitive personal data like banking platforms, government portals, and other essential digital infrastructure. In fact, the website of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, is currently inaccessible due to the certificate being revoked. The site, available at URL https://t.co/czL4wcMGOK says the website Peer’s Certificate has been revoked and that “Someone pretending to be the site could try to steal things like credit card info, passwords, or emails.” The website of Higher Education Department, Government of Kerala, remains inaccessible as well. At this moment, a message is being shown stating that the website might be impersonating https://t.co/QHfKSM1D2j, to steal “your personal and financial information”. Both of these websites were given certificates by eMudhra.

When it comes to cybersecurity infrastructure, every response must be systematic, organised, transparent, and rigorous. The security of India's digital ecosystem cannot depend solely on independent researchers discovering critical failures. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) must undertake a close examination of the role played by the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) in the country’s public key infrastructure. The CCA, appointed under Section 17 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, is responsible for regulating licensed Certifying Authorities within the statutory framework.

In light of the incident, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon the CCA, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), CERT-In, and other relevant authorities to take the following steps.

1. Initiate an independent investigation into the reported compromise, as well as the key generation of other licenses CAs. The investigation should examine compliance with Sections 18, 30 and 31 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the applicable provisions of the Information Technology (Certifying Authorities) Rules, 2000. Failure to meet the prescribed criteria should result in revocation of the Certifying Authority’s license.

2. Strengthen technical audits of Certifying Authorities. Under the CCA's audit criteria, external audits are conducted annually and internal audits every six months. The audits, under CCA’s PKI framework, explicitly looks at whether the CA "maintains controls to provide reasonable assurance that CA key pairs are generated in accordance with industry standards." If the reported weaknesses persisted undetected for an extended period despite the audits, the CCA should review the effectiveness of existing audits under the applicable Certifying Authorities Rules and its Audit Criteria for Certifying Authorities. It must be established whether these audit mechanisms adequately tested cryptographic key generation, key management, certificate issuance, and revocation. The audits should include independent and automated verification of cryptographic key strength, randomness, and key-generation procedures.

3. Improve certificate transparency and independent monitoring. The CCA already maintains a framework of technical requirements, including its Guidelines for Issuance of SSL Certificates, X.509 Certificate Policy for India PKI, and Audit Criteria for Certifying Authorities. These frameworks address certificate management, key management, and technical security controls.

4. Issue actionable mitigation guidance to affected institutions. The CCA and CERT-In should coordinate with affected Certifying Authorities, browsers, and infrastructure providers to communicate actionable guidance to government departments, financial institutions, service providers, and other organisations that may rely on affected certificates. CCA should assess whether their implementation and independent verification are sufficient to detect cryptographic weaknesses of the kind reported in the eMudhra incident.

Statement : CERT-In needs to stop spamming vague and alarming cybersec alerts

October 22, 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned about government SMS messages circulated in English and Hindi under the sender ID AD-ARWGOV-S (Screenshot 1 and 2). These messages invoke CSK and CERT-In, advise recipients to keep their devices free of botnets and malware, and ask them to download a free removal tool from https://t.co/mUQthB2Kd9. The screenshots also show repeated messages from the same sender warning of imprisonment and fines for fraudulently obtaining SIMs or telecom services.

The malware advisory provides no finding about the recipient’s device. Yet the linked website tells visitors their device is “probably infected”, while its FAQ says their internet service provider has been notified (Screenshot 3). Receiving a generic SMS or visiting this public webpage does not establish an infection. Presenting general awareness messages this way risks causing needless panic and making recipients believe their devices have been individually identified as compromised.

There are also concerns about M-Kavach 2, one of the recommended tools. Its Google Play listing declares “No data collected”, while its linked Android privacy policy describes collecting device identifiers and installed-app details and transmitting this information for analysis. C-DAC must explain this discrepancy and disclose access, security and retention safeguards. 

CERT-In must immediately correct the website and clearly distinguish general advisories from evidence-based infection alerts. Encouraging software downloads through unsolicited SMS links risks normalising behaviour that scammers exploit. Government-recommended tools must remain voluntary, minimise permissions and data collection, and undergo independent security and privacy audits with published findings.

We urge the nodal ministry, MEITY to redirect its resourses from political censorship towards the cyber security of ordinary Indians.

The private keys of eight certificate authorities run by eMudhra could be worked out by anyone from the public certificates. eMudhra is a Bengaluru company licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) to issue digital signature certificates in India. On 21 October 2026, we wrote to eMudhra, CERT-In and MeitY seeking an incident report, an independent audit, fuller disclosure from CERT-In and a regulatory inquiry. (1/8)

Read More: https://t.co/zaz71nGqII

We have asked eMudhra to publish a complete incident report and to re-verify every key ceremony it has run, including those for the licensed Indian hierarchy. We have also asked it to commission an independent audit by an auditor it has not engaged before, to notify affected subscribers, and to correct its press release. We have asked CERT-In to say when it received eMudhra's report. We have asked MeitY and the CCA to open an inquiry under Sections 28 and 29 of the IT Act and to verify independently that the Indian hierarchy was untouched. (7/8)

For most people, the fix arrives through ordinary updates. Keep your browser, operating system and phone up to date, never click through a certificate warning, and ignore any unsolicited message offering a "certificate fix". If you run a website with an emSign certificate, check whether it chains to the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and replace it before 27 October. If you build software, update every certificate bundle you depend on and rebuild your container images. (8/8)

Statement : SBI has told the stock exchanges about its data breach, but not the customers whose data was leaked

New Delhi, 21 October 2026

Today, the State Bank of India told the BSE and the National Stock Exchange, in a disclosure under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, that it has experienced an incident involving the loss of customer data. On 16 October 2026 the bank received alerts from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In that its customers’ data was available on the dark web. Its preliminary analysis of about 3.75 lakh records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. These include registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs and details linked to loan records. The bank says it does not yet know where the data came from, and it has engaged a CERT-In empanelled agency to find out.

SBI did not detect this breach itself and learnt of it from outside agencies after the data had already been published. On the same day, a threat monitoring account on X flagged a claim by a group calling itself “Siriusim” that it had released 3.75 lakh rows of SBI data and 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications and account opening forms. The bank’s disclosure does not mention these documents. It also does not say what the remaining records, beyond the 3,897 it has identified, contain.

At the time of this statement, SBI has not said that it has informed any of the affected customers, and its disclosure is silent on the point. Five days passed between the alert and today’s filing. The filing assures investors that the incident has no material impact on the bank’s operations, financial performance or business continuity. However, it does not state anything to the 3,897 people whose phone numbers, dates of birth and home addresses are now with fraudsters. These customers are the most likely to receive calls from persons posing as SBI officials who can recite their account details back to them. A customer cannot guard against a fraud she has not been warned of.

The Internet Freedom Foundation calls on SBI to inform every affected customer directly and without further delay.

We regret to note that the law in force today does not compel the bank to do so. Section 8(6) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a Data Fiduciary to intimate a personal data breach to the Data Protection Board and to each affected Data Principal, and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules, 2025 prescribes how this is to be done. But the Union Government chose a staggered commencement, and these provisions will take effect only on 13 May 2027, nearly four years after Parliament enacted the law. The reporting obligations that apply today, under the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 and the RBI’s cyber security framework for banks, are owed to regulators and not to customers. A listed bank is bound to keep the stock exchanges informed. No law in force clearly binds it to inform the people whose data it holds.

Our demands

1. SBI must inform each affected customer by SMS, email and letter to the registered address, in English, Hindi and the language of the customer’s branch, stating what data was exposed and what steps they should take. It should open a dedicated helpline and an online facility for customers to check whether their data is affected.

2. SBI must state what the 3.75 lakh records and the 2,722 documents contain, how many customers they relate to, and whether they include KYC documents such as Aadhaar, PAN or passport copies.

3. When the investigation concludes, SBI must disclose how the data left its systems, including whether it came through a vendor or a direct selling agent, and publish a summary of the investigating agency’s findings.

4. The Reserve Bank of India should direct all regulated entities to notify customers of personal data breaches within a fixed period, pending the commencement of the DPDP Act.

5. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology should bring Section 8(6) of the DPDP Act and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules into force immediately.

On 21 October 2026, the State Bank of India told the BSE and NSE that 3,897 customer records containing personal data had been found on the dark web. The filing reassures investors that the bank's core business is unaffected. It does not say whether a single affected customer has been told. (1/7)

Yet the RBI has already set the standard. Its Advisory No. 3/2026 of 25 March 2026 records the practice of notifying affected customers through SMS, email, app alerts, calls and website updates, with helpline support. The advisory is not binding, but SBI's filing does not show that the bank has met the standard its own regulator has set out. (6/7)

We have sent a representation to the Chairman of SBI, with copies to the RBI Governor and the Director General of CERT-In, asking SBI to inform every affected customer directly, set up a helpline, and disclose the full scope of the exposure and how the data left the bank. We have asked the RBI to make breach notification binding on regulated entities. If you bank with SBI, treat any message quoting your personal or loan details with care, and report fraud on 1930 or at https://t.co/vQGlyEkV4J. (7/7)
